title: Last jobs, no-show guitarists, marching band and an old horn
summary: Schilling recalls his last jobs, a Mardi Gras no-show, his carnival-ball and marching bands and their players, then talk of doctors, land and an old valve trombone and photos.

story.theme_name: Brass bands, parades and jazz funerals
story.community_name: Parading for Mardi Gras and the clubs

blocks.x: Yeah, on a New Year's Eve night, playing for this big lumberman up in Kansas, the only girl for pleasure, yeah, I'll go play. They had to hire six men for New Year's Eve, that was the union's law. I wouldn't have got in on that job, because he hadn't made a contract before, the union said they had to have six. So they got me on bass and another fellow on guitar, some Italian fellow. They went there and the job paid thirty dollars. Each hour overtime was ten dollars an hour, we would pay three hours overtime. That was the last job, we paid sixty dollars on the union's Eve night. Last job we played, huh? Yeah, he had venison sausage made out of dim eating. Oh man, that big guy had everything you could imagine. That was really the last job that I had played. I had a job one time with him over at Ackerman, you know, he was the president of this here Oak, of the Colton Cornwall Club, and here they are. Cap, he had a reception there, he hired Tony Capone with four pieces. Me, Tony Capone, a guitar player and Charlie Fishbein. Well the guitar player never did show up. Now you know what the rhythm I had, the bass in them. I had that, I had that, that happened to me on Mardi Gras Day. Yeah, I had a rhythm on the bass in them, and they never had a talk of them one time. That happened to me on one of those stands on Canal Street Mardi Gras Day, the little Chink Martin Jr. didn't show up. Bass? No, on guitar. On guitar. We had a bass, we had Sherwood Manjapani on bass. Yeah, he did. And little Chink Martin was supposed to come on guitar, and he came whimpering around, I couldn't get a hold of a guitar, Johnny. Couldn't get a hold of a guitar. Boy, I let out at him, I'm telling you. I sure let him know what I thought about. This day when they shut up one. They don't care a thing about what they do, you know. I mean ruin your whole band for the whole day. They had to struggle up there for what, six hours? I don't know what it was, but struggling up there without any harmony at all, except from the bass fiddle. You like that? Yeah, yeah, yeah. Three front lines and a bass fiddle. Four pieces, you see. Boy, that's a lot of fun to have to struggle through that for six hours. The rhythm is out, you just got a bass fiddle in and whoop where you have to. You got a little harmony, you know, so you can attach yourself to that harmony all right, but I mean after all there's not enough harmony in the bass fiddle. But this, I asked Tony, I said, what happened to the day I was just getting there? I said, he think it was tomorrow night. Remember how I used to do them guys in the spot jobs? Used to make a mistake, I had a little notebook, a slip of paper, and make a job. I had a band one time, Johnny, before you played with me. I was in such a demand, people used to ring me up what date you got up so we can give a dance. I'm not kidding you. That's true. You used to have a whole bunch of bands. That's true, they used to ring me up what date you got up when you were dancing. This guy had all the music tied up in the audience. That's right. I had the boys of Bahamians, had Hermes, and I was the first band playing Hermes, I still got to one of the seven years in there yet. All the different carnival balls. Those were the balls, did you do much of the parade work too? Oh that parade work. Oh did he? Yeah. Boy I was right up in the head. He had everything, he had a whole bunch of bands out. I had one of the best marching bands in the city, for the ten men. The men in my lineup was this, Harry Shannon, you didn't know him. Oh. You know Leon Danena. Yeah. He played trumpet. Harry Shannon. Danena played trumpet. He was a piano player and one of the best bass players in town, did you know that? The piano man? I'm talking about the- The fellow that's directing the police band today. Danena used to be at Four Chain High School? He's got the police band- He's a trumpet player? Well I said he played with me. Oh God I say. I'll tell you. He played trumpet with me, he played string bass with me, he played piano, you ask him. Every time I meet them, you know what he does to me? What? He was a player, he was playing a dedication with the police band. I left there looking and he was getting ready to start the bass. I left the whole way. Who else did you have in your marching band? I had a little, uh, Melon Bonina, Georgia Board, and, uh, Harry Shannon, who was my three trumpets. I had a fellow named Johnny Getty playing alto horn, a peck horn, and one peck horn. I had a fellow named Bob. Fred Dan Tagner playing alto saxophone, Georgia played- Who was on alto saxophone? Fred Dan Tagner. Oh. He used to play with Buckethead. Oh I know, yeah. He used to play with us in Texas. Oh man, powerful. Yeah. He was powerful. Wonderful attack. And then, when George was playing center saxophone, this was supposed to be a brass band, man, they were heavy. And they had, uh, Eddie Iman from Pace, a suit of phone, he bought that suit of phone from Mackey. Lefty Iman. He bought that suit of phone from Mackey. Red Mackey. Red Mackey, yeah. He still got the same suit of phone yet, I believe. Well I had, uh, a fellow by the name of, playing bass drum, and had Frisco on snare drum, and this fellow playing bass drum, Spora. He was a good man. Not Spobora. And we used to play like- Not Tony Spargo, Spobora. No, Spora. Spora, Spora, Spora, yeah. He was an old time bass drum. Yeah. And, uh, we used to play with Heather Morrissey, he even got the Morrissey from the Shrine Band, on the card. Yeah. Tent Commanders, all that big moorers. You see us coming down that street there. We was coming around, we was coming around, making a turn into Canal Street, and Ralph Shabawa was the secretary of union. He looked up to me and said I thought they were claiming and then bang, all of us, you know how the boys, they'd sooner play music than each. They were, 90% of them weren't playing for money. It was just, just, just that place. I don't know what they were, but that was it. Man, they fucked proud. I said they had red ribbons on the end of my drum, and I was shaking. You all smoking? No thanks, I remember the insurance. Well, tell me I'm glad you come around. The doctor, the doctor still lets you smoke, huh boy? Man, I smoke a cotton cell the rest of the week. I don't go food to no doctors, they're waiting them guys, you better off. My wife just went through that hospital clinic jail, and they fell around and busted their head wide open, and I brought her up there in the morning and said, that wasn't the cause of the cause of the cause of the give me Debbie, the one right there. Went through all those tests, and he gave her some little beef pills. She had a blood clot on the opposite side of the head. Oh, really? Yeah. That's fine. You have to watch that. It's a good thing he went there. You're going to go to the doctors and not me. When I, one time I had a play, I had four places over, over, over, over. The county, you know, part one, solo one, part one, solo one, and one of them was a dog on one of them. I had to give them away. And I was cutting grass with an electric plumber. You know, I said, I got short ones. I shot an electric more on Sunday, that's the grass. Let the grass grow. That was it. That was it. When you grew up with the grass, I thought something was going to hurt me. Well, that's all right if you've got sense enough to do that, you see. But a lot of people keep on going. You know, after that they go rest up and then they go back to it. Well, you don't have to go to a doctor if you do that, because the doctor is going to tell you to do that. I've been running over the covers for 20 years. But I had a place at Military Road, I had a place at McCombs, I had a place, I had two places in Chinchube and one on the Madisonville Harbor was the last place I sold. And I had a couple pieces of ground. I sold and sold it all. I'm in money. I bought one a lot for $50 and sold it for $4.50. I bought one for $100 and sold it for $1,000. It was the last piece I sold. I thought the cars were going to come through and get a boom, boom, boom, boom. Well, everything did go up. But they said there wasn't much of it to sell it, nobody could sell it. I was talking to the old Dean of Deanna. You got it here? Yeah. You got it here? Back of the garage there. You don't want to get it? And each flat trombone. Each flat valve trombone. We used to play it with Jack Ray when I pushed out the plate and he used to be, oh, what are you going to do with this? Look at this. You know that? Oh. You know that? Oh, yes, I have one of those. You know? I hope I still have it. Is that your one? He sent me one once. Is that your old? Yes. That's my old. I haven't seen that. Well, ain't you in this picture, Mr. Russell? Oh, look at this. Chris Hackney Show. That's in 1925, huh, Hackney? Was that 25? No. No. No. I played violin. I know you ain't, but the Souchant is a... Yes, Souchant. Here's Souchant right here. And here's Earl Crom. Yeah, I remember that. I remember that. I remember that. Yeah. You mentioned my old boy. I remember that. I remember that. Yeah. You mentioned my old boy. I remember that. I remember that. Yeah. I remember that. Yeah. I remember that. I remember that. Yeah. You mentioned my name, all of the sort of stories. Mm-hmm. Yeah. I shoved them on the side. Let me go see if I can get them. Sure, I'll let the rest of them have been. Mm-hmm . Tutula Akhenna's father. This is George's son. And here's Elrin Mazur, the fellow who played clarinet with me on that Victor record. You know, the ex- I've got this date on the tape there on here. It was September 28, 1952. And that's the... I have one. You sent me one. I'm hoping I didn't loan that to John Snyder and that he kept it. I haven't seen that for a few years. I must have it at home. I sure haven't seen it for a while. I know I have. Do you want to read it again, John? No, no. I got it at home. That's the old horn. Oh, look at that. I got it real short. I thought it would be any longer. Fifty-four years old. Now, is that how it isn't Ben? You had that fifty-four years. You had that fifty-four years. No, no. Is that the same kind of going on in 52? Is that the same pinch as an outdoor horn, Ben? I can eat that outdoor. Is that a silver horn? No. No. Gold brass. Gold brass. I want to show you to leave them. No. We should pass him up over here. Yeah, I see his pictures. Yeah, I see his pictures. Yeah. I can wear a lot of mouthpiece for a room. See, I'd like to see how I get a couple of notes on it. Huh? Go ahead. Well listen, that thing is hard to play that high pitch on. You don't like those high pitch on, do you? You like the B flat, don't you? Yeah, the B flat. The B flat's better. I can't wait to try it.
